also: why did he chew you out?

evidence: Cic. Cael. 25: objurgāvit M. Caelium, sīcut nēminem umquam parēns (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: to chide, scold, rebuke (frequent and classical).

evidence: Plaut. Most. 3.2.63: numquid increpāvit fīlium? (Lewis & Short s.v. increpō)
terms.comment: Literally “make a noise at”: a sharp, loud rebuke. Objūrgāre is the everyday word.

evidence: Petr. 43.4: malam parram pilāvit (Lewis & Short, a doubtful reading)
terms.comment: Traupman gives it for “why did the instructor chew you out?”. Lewis & Short knows pilāre only as to strip of hair and, rarely and late, to plunder; it is not a word for scolding.

phrases.latin: monendī amīcī saepe sunt et objurgandī
phrases.english: friends must often be advised, and told off

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 95, checked against the searchable text and the page images of the book.: p. 290.
